title: Testing
summary: Tests you can trust: spot the test that checks nothing, then fix it with real Jest assertions, awaited promises, clean setup and well-checked mocks.

lessons.title: What makes a test effective?
lessons.objective: With a block of code and the associated Unit Test, determine where the test is ineffective and modify it to make it more effective.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **unit test** runs one small piece of code, like a function, and checks the result. A good test fails when the code is broken. It passes when the code works. A weak test passes either way, so it gives you false comfort.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A smoke alarm. A good one beeps for a real fire and stays quiet for toast. A broken one never beeps, so the room looks safe. Where it stops: a test only checks what you told it to check. It can't notice anything else.

cards.title: Three sizes of test
items: **Unit test**: one function on its own. Its helpers are often swapped for fakes.
**Integration test**: several real parts working together, like a service and its database.
**End-to-end test**: the whole app, driven like a user in a real browser.

cards.title: Two ways to plan a test
cards.body: **Black-box** tests use only inputs and outputs. You never read the code. **White-box** tests are planned with the code open, so every inner path gets a turn. Example: the code checks `age > 18`, so a white-box tester makes sure to try 18 and 19.

cards.title: Two ways a test lies
cards.body: Count a pass as "positive: the code works". A **false positive** passes while the code is broken, often because nothing real is checked. A **false negative** fails while the code works. Example: a test reads a private helper by name, and a safe rename breaks it. Some books swap the two labels, so learn the situations.

cards.title: A test that checks nothing
cards.body: `=>` makes a small function, and `===` means "exactly equal". `console.assert` only writes a message when its check is false. It never fails the test. So this test is green even when `addTax` is broken. Use `expect(total).toBe(110)` instead: it fails unless `total` is `110`.

cards.title: An effective test
items: Has a real **assertion** on the actual result: `expect()` takes it and `toBe()` checks it, as in `expect(x).toBe(3)`.
Covers **edge cases**: empty input, `null` (no value), zero, the values right at a limit, and errors.
Checks what users see, not **implementation details** (private names, inner steps).
Stands alone: fresh data each time, no order between tests.

cards.title: Exam trap
cards.body: "The test is green, so the code works." Not always. Some tests stay green while the code is broken: no assertion, a vague one like `toBeDefined()` (anything but `undefined` passes), or only easy inputs. The exam shows such a test and asks for the change that would catch the bug.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Break it to trust it."** Break the code on purpose for a moment. If the test stays green, it checks nothing, so fix the test.

terms.say: A small test for one piece of code, like one function. Its helpers are often swapped for fakes, so only that piece is checked.
A test that checks several real parts working together, like a service saving to a real test database.
A test that uses the whole app the way a person would, clicking through a real browser from start to finish.
Testing a thing only by what goes in and what comes out. You never look inside the code.
Testing with the code open in front of you. You pick inputs so every inner path and branch gets a turn.
A test that says "all good" while the code is really broken. It passes when it should fail.
A test that fails even though the code works fine. It often happens after a safe rename the test depended on.
The private inside parts of code, like helper names or inner steps. Users never see them, so tests shouldn't depend on them.
The line in a test that checks a result, like expect(total).toBe(110). If the check is false, the test fails.
Unusual inputs at the edges, like an empty list, null, zero or the exact limit. Bugs love to hide there.
An arrow that makes a small function. () => { ... } is a function with no inputs. The code inside the braces runs each time the function is called.
Checks if two values are exactly the same, type included. 110 === 110 is true, but 110 === '110' is false, because one is text.
Checks a condition and writes an error message to the console only when it is false. It never stops the code and never fails a Jest test.
Jest's way to start a check. You put the real value inside, then add a matcher, like expect(2 + 2).toBe(4).
A Jest check that passes only for the exact same value. expect(3).toBe(3) passes, expect(3).toBe(4) fails.
A Jest check that only asks: is this value something other than undefined? 0, null and wrong numbers all pass, so it catches very little.
A special value that means "nothing here, on purpose". Code often forgets about it, so it makes a good edge case to test.

lessons.title: Jest: matchers, setup and async tests
lessons.objective: With a block of code and the associated Unit Test, determine where the test is ineffective and modify it to make it more effective.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Jest** is a popular tool that runs JavaScript tests and reports pass or fail. Add it with `npm install --save-dev jest`. npm is Node's package installer. `--save-dev` lists Jest as a tool for building and testing, not for the live app. Then add `"test": "jest"` to `scripts` in `package.json` and run `npm test`.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A referee with a rule book. `expect(value)` says "look at this". The **matcher**, like `toBe(3)`, is the rule it must meet. Where it stops: the referee only judges the moments you point at. Code you never check is never judged.

cards.title: A first test
cards.body: `require()` loads the `sum` function from the file `sum.js`. `describe()` groups tests under a name. `test()` (or its twin `it()`) holds one test: a name, then a function to run. `expect(sum(1, 2)).toBe(3)` passes only if `sum` gives `3`. Jest finds files ending in `.test.js` by itself.

cards.title: Pick the right matcher
items: `toBe()`: the exact same value, like `3`, or the very same object.
`toEqual()`: compares what's inside objects and arrays. Skips properties set to `undefined`.
`toStrictEqual()`: like `toEqual()`, but `undefined` properties count, and the class must match.
`toBeCloseTo()`: for decimals, since `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`.
`toThrow()`: checks that a function throws. Pass a function: `expect(() => fn()).toThrow()`.

cards.title: Async tests: wait for it
cards.body: A **promise** is a value that arrives later. **Return or await** it, so Jest waits. Otherwise the test ends before the promise settles (finishes), and it passes by mistake. `.resolves` checks the value a promise gives. `.rejects` checks the error it fails with. `async` lets a function use `await`.

cards.title: Count the checks
cards.body: `.catch()` runs only when a promise fails. If `checkout` wrongly succeeds, the check inside never runs, and a test with no checks passes. `expect.assertions(1)` says exactly one check must run, so now this test fails instead.

cards.title: Setup and teardown
cards.body: `beforeEach()` and `afterEach()` run around **every** test. `beforeAll()` and `afterAll()` run **once** per file, or once per `describe` block they sit in. So with 3 tests, `beforeEach()` runs 3 times and `beforeAll()` runs once. Build fresh data in `beforeEach()` so no test leans on another.

cards.title: Exam trap
cards.body: `expect(parse('x')).toThrow()` looks right but isn't. `parse` runs first and throws inside the test, before `toThrow()` can catch it. Wrap the call in a function: `expect(() => parse('x')).toThrow()`. And `toBe()` on two equal-looking objects fails, because they are different objects.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Same box: toBe. Same stuff: toEqual. Async: await. Throw: wrap."**

terms.say: A tool that runs JavaScript tests and tells you which ones passed and which ones failed.
The checking word after expect, like toBe or toEqual. It says what the value must be for the test to pass.
A Jest function that groups related tests under one name, so the report is tidy and setup can be shared.
A Jest matcher that passes only for the same value, or the very same object. Two lookalike objects are not the same object.
A Jest matcher that compares what is inside objects and arrays, piece by piece. It skips properties whose value is undefined.
Like toEqual, but fussier. Undefined properties count, and a class object doesn't equal a plain object with the same fields.
A Jest matcher that checks a function throws an error. You hand it a function to call, not the result of a call.
How a test tells Jest to wait for a promise. Without it, Jest ends the test before the promise is done.
Jest hooks: beforeEach runs before every test in its file or describe block, and afterEach runs after every one. Great for fresh test data and clean-up.
Tells Jest exactly how many checks must run in a test. If a check inside a callback never runs, the test fails instead of passing.
Loads code from another file so you can use it here. require('./sum') gives you what the file sum.js shares.
Jest's function for one test. You give it a name and a function with the checks. it() is the same thing with a shorter name.
A Jest check for decimals. It passes when two numbers are almost equal, so 0.1 + 0.2 counts as 0.3.
A value that isn't ready yet, like a ticket for food that's still cooking. Later it either gives a value or fails with an error.
async goes before a function and makes it give back a promise. Inside it, await pauses until a promise is done, then hands you its value.
Goes after expect on a promise. It waits for the promise's value, then checks it, like .resolves.toBe(5). It fails if the promise fails.
Goes after expect on a promise that should fail. It waits for the error, then checks it, like .rejects.toThrow('Bad id'). It fails if the promise succeeds.
Runs a function only when a promise fails, and hands it the error. If the promise succeeds, that function never runs.
Jest hooks that run only once: beforeAll before the first test in its file or describe block, afterAll after the last. Good for slow, shared setup.

lessons.title: Test doubles: mocks, spies and fake timers
lessons.objective: With a block of code and the associated Unit Test, determine where the test is ineffective and modify it to make it more effective.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **test double** stands in for something real your code uses, like a web service, a database or a timer. It makes tests fast and repeatable. It also lets you check how your code used it: called or not, how often, with what.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A stunt double in a film. The star stays safe while the double does the risky part. Where it stops: a Jest double also takes notes. It writes down every call, so your test can check them afterwards.

cards.title: Kinds of doubles
items: **Stub**: gives ready-made answers, like always `true`.
**Spy**: records the calls it gets.
**Mock**: a fake set up with what it should get and give, then checked.
In Jest: `jest.fn()` makes a new fake function. `jest.spyOn(obj, 'method')` watches a real method. `jest.mock('./api')` swaps a whole module (a code file) for a fake.

cards.title: A mock function
cards.body: `send` is a fake function that returns `true` every time. After `notify` runs, `toHaveBeenCalledTimes()` checks that `send` ran once. `toHaveBeenCalledWith()` checks that it got `'ana@site.co'`. Every call is also saved in `send.mock.calls`.

cards.title: Tell a fake what to do
items: `mockReturnValue()`: every call returns the value you give, like `mockReturnValue(true)`.
`mockReturnValueOnce()`: only the next call returns it. Once values are used first, in order.
`mockResolvedValue()`: each call returns a promise that gives the value.
`mockImplementation()`: each call runs your own function instead.

cards.title: Spies and clean-up
cards.body: `jest.spyOn` still calls the **real method** unless you give it fake behavior with `.mockImplementation()` or `.mockReturnValue()`. Between tests, `jest.clearAllMocks()` wipes the call records. `jest.resetAllMocks()` also drops the fake return values. `jest.restoreAllMocks()` puts back the original methods that spies wrapped.

cards.title: Fake timers
cards.body: `setTimeout()` runs code later: `setTimeout(save, 1000)` calls `save` after 1000 ms (one second). **Fake timers**, turned on by `jest.useFakeTimers()`, mean nothing really waits. `jest.advanceTimersByTime()` moves the fake clock, so `save` runs at once. `jest.runAllTimers()` runs every waiting timer.

cards.title: Exam trap
cards.body: A mock that is never checked proves nothing. `expect(send).toBeDefined()` passes even if your code never calls `send`. Check the call itself with `toHaveBeenCalledWith()`. Old short names like `toBeCalledWith` were removed in Jest 30, so learn the full `toHaveBeenCalled…` names.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Fake it, then check it."** Every double needs an `expect` on how it was used. Clean up between tests.

terms.say: A pretend version of something your code uses, like a fake web API. It makes tests fast and lets you see how it was used.
A pretend helper that always gives the same ready-made answer. It doesn't keep notes about how it was used.
A helper that watches calls and writes them down: how many, and with what. In Jest, a spy can still run the real code.
A fake set up ahead of time with what it should receive and give back. Your test then checks it was used that way.
Makes a brand-new fake function. It remembers every call, and you can tell it what to return.
Watches a real method on an object. By default the real method still runs, and every call is recorded.
Swaps a whole module for a fake one in a test file, so its functions become mock functions.
The original code of a function, not a fake. A Jest spy keeps calling it unless you give the spy fake behavior.
A pretend clock, turned on with jest.useFakeTimers(). Then setTimeout and setInterval wait for your test to move time forward, so nothing really waits.
Wipes the call records of every mock but keeps their fake return values. Handy between tests.
A Jest check for how many times a fake function was called. toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) passes only if it ran exactly once.
A Jest check that a fake function was called with certain values, like toHaveBeenCalledWith('ana@site.co'). It passes if any one call matches.
Tells a fake function what to give back. mockReturnValue(true) sets every call. mockReturnValueOnce sets just the next call, and those are used first.
Makes a fake function return a promise that gives a value. mockResolvedValue(5) works like returning Promise.resolve(5).
Gives a fake function your own code to run on each call. With mockImplementation((n) => n * 2), calling it with 3 gives 6.
Wipes every mock's call records and also its fake return values. After it, a plain mock returns undefined until you set it up again.
Puts the real methods back on objects where jest.spyOn had wrapped them. After it, calls go to the original code again.
Runs a function later, after a wait in milliseconds. setTimeout(save, 1000) calls save after about one second.
With fake timers on, moves the pretend clock forward. Any timer whose time comes up runs right away.
With fake timers on, runs every waiting timer right now, however long each was set to wait.

flashcards.front: What does an effective unit test do?
flashcards.back: It fails when the code is broken and passes when it works. It checks the real result with `expect`, covers edge cases and runs on its own.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between unit, integration and end-to-end tests?
flashcards.back: Unit: one piece on its own. Integration: several real parts together. End-to-end: the whole app, used like a person would in a browser.
No. It only writes a message to the console when its condition is false. The test still passes. Use `expect` instead.

flashcards.front: What is a false positive in testing?
flashcards.back: A test that passes while the code is broken, often because nothing real is checked. A false negative fails while the code works. Some books swap the labels.
`toBe` for primitives or the very same object. `toEqual` to compare contents deeply. `toStrictEqual` to also check `undefined` properties and class types.

flashcards.front: How do you test that a function throws in Jest?
flashcards.back: Wrap the call in a function: `expect(() => parse('x')).toThrow()`. Calling it directly throws before `expect` can catch it.

flashcards.front: Why can an async Jest test pass by mistake?
flashcards.back: If the test doesn't return or await the promise, Jest ends the test before the promise finishes. The check runs too late to count.
`beforeEach` runs before every test in its file or `describe` block. `beforeAll` runs once, before the first of those tests.

flashcards.front: What does `jest.fn()` give you in a test?
flashcards.back: A fake function that records each call in `mock.calls`. You can set what it returns with `mockReturnValue` or `mockResolvedValue`.
No. By default it records calls and still runs the real method. Add `mockImplementation` or `mockReturnValue` to replace it.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `clearAllMocks`, `resetAllMocks` and `restoreAllMocks`?
flashcards.back: Clear wipes the call records. Reset also drops the fake return values. Restore puts back real methods that `jest.spyOn` wrapped.

flashcards.front: How do you test code that uses `setTimeout` without waiting?
flashcards.back: Call `jest.useFakeTimers()` to swap in a pretend clock. Then move time with `jest.advanceTimersByTime(ms)`, or run every waiting timer with `jest.runAllTimers()`.

questions.q: Which statement describes a unit test?
options: It runs the whole app in a real browser, the way a user would
It checks one small piece of code, like a function, on its own
It checks that several real modules and services work together correctly
It measures how fast a page loads under heavy traffic
questions.explain: A unit test checks one small unit of code on its own. Anything it depends on is usually swapped for a fake.
wrong: That is an end-to-end test.
That is an integration test.
That is a load or performance test, not a unit test.
questions.source: Trailhead: Cert Prep: JavaScript Dev: Debugging, Error Handling, and Testing

questions.q: The `addTax` function has a bug. What happens when Jest runs this test?
options: The test fails, and Jest shows the message from the assert
Jest marks the test as skipped because it has no `expect`
The test passes, and a message is written to the console
The test fails with a timeout after five seconds
questions.explain: `console.assert` only writes a message when its condition is false. It never fails the test, so the broken code still gets a green test.
wrong: `console.assert` only logs; it doesn't throw, so the test can't fail from it.
Jest runs tests without an `expect`; it doesn't skip them.
Nothing here waits, so there is no timeout.

questions.q: A tester checks a `formatPrice` function only by giving it inputs and comparing the outputs. They never read its code. Which kind of testing is this?
questions.explain: Black-box testing uses only inputs and outputs, without looking inside the code.
wrong: White-box tests are designed from the code's inner paths.
Integration tests check several real parts together; this is one function.
Snapshot tests compare output to a saved copy; reading the code isn't the point.
questions.source: Trailhead: Cert Prep: JavaScript Dev: Debugging, Error Handling, and Testing

questions.q: The rule says anyone aged 18 or older is an adult. This test passes. Which added line would catch the bug?
questions.explain: Bugs hide at the edges, so test the exact limit. `isAdult(18)` returns `false` here, so this line fails and exposes the bug.
wrong: 40 is far from the limit; the buggy code still returns `true`.
17 gives `false` with or without the bug.
5 is far from the limit; the buggy code still returns `false`.

questions.q: A team reviews its unit tests. Which two habits make a test more effective? (Choose 2)
options: Assert on the actual result with `expect`
Share one changing object across all the tests in a file
Add edge cases such as an empty list and `null`
Print the result with `console.log` and check it by eye
Check private helper values instead of the public result
questions.explain: An effective test asserts the real result and covers the edge cases. Bugs often hide in empty, missing or boundary inputs.
wrong: Shared changing data makes tests depend on each other and on their order.
A log never fails a test, so a broken result can slip by.
Private details change in safe refactors, which breaks the test for no reason.
questions.source: Trailhead: Cert Prep: JavaScript Dev: Debugging, Error Handling, and Testing

questions.q: A developer renames an internal helper. The app still works for users, but a test that called that helper by name now fails. In Kent C. Dodds' terms (the reading the Cert Prep unit links), what is this result?
options: A flaky test that fails at random
questions.explain: A false negative is a test that fails while the code works. It often happens when a test depends on private details, like a helper's name, and a safe rename breaks it.
wrong: A false positive passes while the code is broken; this test failed while the code works.
A true negative would mean the code really is broken.
A flaky test passes and fails at random; this one fails every time.
questions.source: Kent C. Dodds: Testing Implementation Details

questions.q: `applyDiscount(cart, 0.1)` should lower `cart.total` from 100 to 90. A teammate says it does nothing, yet this test is green. Which change makes the test catch the bug?
questions.explain: A test must assert the actual expected result. `toBeDefined()` passes for 100 as well as 90, so only `toBe(90)` catches the bug.
wrong: Any object is truthy, so this passes even when nothing changed.
100 is not `null`, so this passes even when nothing changed.
A function that does nothing doesn't throw, so this passes too.

questions.q: `addItem` works correctly, yet the second test fails. What is the best fix?
options: Rename the tests so they run in a different order
Create a fresh `list` in a `beforeEach` hook
questions.explain: Tests must not share changing data. The second test sees the item left by the first, so it gets 3 items; a fresh list in `beforeEach` fixes that.
wrong: `afterAll` runs once after all the tests, too late to help.
`toEqual(2)` compares the whole array to the number 2, so it fails too.
Test names don't decide the order, and order-based fixes are fragile.

questions.q: What does `console.assert(false, 'oops')` do?
options: It writes an error message to the console
It throws an error that stops the whole script
It pauses the code like a breakpoint
It marks the current Jest test as failed
questions.explain: `console.assert` writes a message only when its condition is false. It doesn't throw or stop anything.
wrong: It only logs; the script carries on.
Breakpoints come from `debugger` or DevTools, not `console.assert`.
It never fails a test, which is why it is no substitute for `expect`.

questions.q: A test calls `OrderService.save()`, which writes through the real `Database` module to a test database. Then it reads the order back. What kind of test is this?
questions.explain: An integration test checks several real parts working together. Here the service and the real database module both run.
wrong: A unit test would swap the database for a fake.
End-to-end tests drive the whole app through its user interface.
Snapshot tests compare output to a saved copy.
questions.source: Trailhead: Cert Prep: JavaScript Dev: Debugging, Error Handling, and Testing

questions.q: The spec says `getInitials` returns capital initials, and returns `''` for `null` or an empty string. The current test passes. Which two new checks would fail and expose a bug? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: Good tests probe edge cases against the spec. `null` makes `split` throw, and lowercase input returns `'al'`, so both checks fail and reveal bugs.
wrong: This returns `'GH'`, so it passes and finds nothing.
An empty string already returns `''`, so it passes.
This returns `'AT'`, so it passes and finds nothing.

questions.q: Which statement describes white-box testing?
options: Tests use only inputs and outputs and never read the source code
Tests are run by end users before a release
Tests are designed from the code's inner paths and branches
Tests always run in a browser with no window
questions.explain: White-box tests are built with the code in view. You pick inputs so each path and branch runs.
wrong: That is black-box testing.
That describes user acceptance testing.
A browser with no window (headless) is a tool choice, not a kind of test design.
questions.source: Trailhead: Cert Prep: JavaScript Dev: Debugging, Error Handling, and Testing

questions.q: The team plans to rename `_n` to `_count` without changing how `counter` behaves. Which change lets the test survive this rename and any later change to private names?
questions.explain: Test the public behavior, not the private details. `counter.value` stays the same after the rename, so the test won't break for no reason.
wrong: This still depends on a private name, so the next rename breaks it again.
The matcher isn't the problem; the private property is.
Without an assertion the test checks nothing.
questions.source: Trailhead: Cert Prep: JavaScript Dev: Debugging, Error Handling, and Testing

questions.q: The spec says `isTeen(age)` is `true` for ages 13 to 19, both included. The current test passes. Which two new checks would fail and expose a bug? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: Test both edges of the rule. With `>` and `<`, the code returns `false` for 13 and 19, so those two checks fail. Values just outside the range pass either way.
wrong: 12 is outside the range, and the buggy code returns `false` too.
20 is outside the range, and the buggy code returns `false` too.
15 is in the middle, and the buggy code returns `true` too.
questions.source: Trailhead: Cert Prep: JavaScript Dev: Debugging, Error Handling, and Testing

questions.q: A team wants to check that a shopper can sign in, add an item and pay, in a real browser against the running app. Which kind of test fits?
questions.explain: End-to-end tests use the whole app the way a user would, from start to finish.
wrong: A unit test checks one small piece on its own.
An integration test checks a few parts together, not the full user journey.
White-box is a way to design tests, not a test of the full journey.
questions.source: Trailhead: Cert Prep: JavaScript Dev: Debugging, Error Handling, and Testing

questions.q: `makeUser('Ana')` returns `{ name: 'Ana', active: true }`. What happens when this test runs?
options: It passes, because every property has the same value
It fails, because `toBe` checks for the very same object
It fails, because `toBe` only accepts strings and numbers
It passes, because `toBe` compares objects deeply
questions.explain: `toBe` checks for the very same object (it uses `Object.is`). Two separate objects never match, even with equal contents. Use `toEqual` to compare their contents.
wrong: Same values aren't enough for `toBe`; it needs the same object.
`toBe` accepts any value; it just compares identity.
Deep comparison is what `toEqual` does, not `toBe`.

questions.q: What happens when this test runs?
options: It passes, because `parseAge('abc')` really does throw the expected message
It passes, but only if `toThrow` is given the `TypeError` class
It fails, because `toThrow` cannot take a message string
It fails, because `parseAge` throws before `toThrow` can catch it
questions.explain: `toThrow` needs a function to call. Here `parseAge('abc')` runs first and throws inside the test, so the test fails. Write `expect(() => parseAge('abc')).toThrow('Not a number')`.
wrong: The error escapes before `expect` sees it, so the test fails.
The argument doesn't matter; the call isn't wrapped in a function.
`toThrow` accepts a string and checks that the message contains it.

questions.q: `fetchUser(1)` resolves to `{ name: 'Bob' }` after a short delay. Why does Jest report this test as passing?
options: `toBe` treats two different strings as equal inside a `then` callback
Jest silently skips any `expect` written inside a callback function
Nothing returns or awaits the promise, so the test ends first
A test without the `async` keyword can never fail at all
questions.explain: Jest waits only for a promise that the test returns or awaits. Here the test ends first, so the failing check comes too late to count.
wrong: `toBe('Ana')` would fail for `'Bob'` if it ran in time.
Jest runs checks in callbacks; this one simply runs after the test ended.
Tests without `async` fail all the time; the problem is the missing wait.

questions.q: `fetchUser(1)` resolves to `{ name: 'Bob' }` after a short delay, yet this test passes. Which two changes make it fail correctly when the name is wrong? (Choose 2)
options: Raise the test timeout to 10 seconds
Wrap the body of the test in `try...catch`
Make the test `async` and use `const user = await fetchUser(1)` before the `expect`
questions.explain: Returning or awaiting the promise makes Jest wait for it. Then the failing check counts.
wrong: A longer timeout doesn't help if Jest isn't waiting for the promise.
A `try...catch` can't catch a check that runs after the test ended.
It only says zero checks are expected, so the test still passes.

questions.q: `saveOrder(order)` is an `async` function. For an order with no items, it should reject with an `Error` whose message contains `'Missing items'`. Which line tests this correctly?
questions.explain: A promise that fails (rejects) is tested with `.rejects`, and the test must await it. `.rejects.toThrow` then checks the error message.
wrong: `toThrow` needs a function, and a promise isn't one.
`.resolves` expects success, but this promise fails (rejects).
An `async` function doesn't throw when called; it returns a rejected promise.

questions.q: Given `const a = { id: 1, note: undefined }` and `const b = { id: 1 }`, which assertion fails?
questions.explain: `toStrictEqual` counts properties set to `undefined`, but `toEqual` ignores them. So only the strict check fails.
wrong: `toEqual` skips `undefined` properties, so it passes.
Both ids are the number 1, so it passes.
`{ id: 2 }` has a different id, so `not.toStrictEqual` passes.

questions.q: A developer adds Jest to a project. Jest should be used only while building and testing, not in production. Which command fits?
questions.explain: Tools used only for building and testing go in `devDependencies` in `package.json`. `npm install --save-dev jest` puts Jest there.
wrong: A global install isn't recorded in the project, so teammates won't get it.
`--save-prod` puts Jest in regular `dependencies`.
`uninstall` removes a package instead of adding it.

questions.q: What number does the third test log?
questions.explain: `beforeAll` runs once and `beforeEach` runs before every test. By the third test that is 1 + 10 + 10 + 10 = 31.
wrong: `beforeAll` runs once, not before each test.
This misses the single `beforeAll` run.
`beforeEach` has already run three times, not once.

questions.q: What does this test file log at the end?
questions.explain: A top-level `beforeEach` runs before every test, and a hook inside `describe` runs only for that block's tests. Test `a` gets outer then inner; test `b` gets only outer.
wrong: For test `a`, the outer hook runs first, then the inner one; test `b` comes after.
Outer hooks run before inner hooks, not after.
The inner hook doesn't run for test `b`, which is outside the `describe`.

questions.q: `expect(0.1 + 0.2).toBe(0.3)` fails. Which two assertions pass? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004` in JavaScript. `toBeCloseTo` allows a tiny difference; the optional second number sets how many decimal places to check.
wrong: `toEqual` needs the exact number, so the tiny error fails it.
`toStrictEqual` needs the exact number too.
`0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` is `false`, so this fails.

questions.q: `checkout([])` should reject, but a bug makes it resolve. This test still passes. Which change makes it fail as it should?
options: Add `expect.assertions(1)` at the start of the test
Wrap the `return` statement in a `try...catch` block
questions.explain: If the promise succeeds, the `.catch` function never runs, so no check happens. `expect.assertions(1)` makes a test with zero checks fail.
wrong: The promise is already returned; that isn't the gap.
A resolved promise throws nothing, so there is nothing to catch.
The matcher never runs, so changing it changes nothing.

questions.q: With Jest's default settings, which file is picked up as a test file?
questions.explain: By default Jest runs files ending in `.test.js` or `.spec.js`, and any `.js` file inside a `__tests__` folder.
wrong: The suffix must be `.test`, not `.tests`.
`.check` isn't one of the default suffixes.
A `test-` prefix doesn't count outside a `__tests__` folder.

questions.q: Given `const tags = ['js', 'node']`, which assertion passes?
questions.explain: `toContain` checks that an item is in an array. `'node'` is one of the items.
wrong: A new array literal is a different object, so `toBe` fails.
The array holds the string `'node'`, not an array with it.
The array has 2 items, not 3.

questions.q: Given the `Point` class, which two assertions pass? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: `toEqual` compares contents and ignores the class. `toStrictEqual` also checks the class, so it passes only against another `Point` with the same values.
wrong: A `Point` isn't a plain object, so the strict check fails.
Two `new Point` calls make two different objects.
The extra `z` property makes the contents differ.

questions.q: While fixing a bug, a developer wants Jest to run just one test in a file and skip the rest for now. What should they use?
questions.explain: `test.only` runs that test and skips the others in the file. Remove it before you commit (save) your code.
wrong: `test.skip` skips that one test and runs the rest.
`test.todo` marks a test you plan to write later.
`describe.each` runs a block once per row of data.

questions.q: What does `greet.mock.calls` hold after this code runs?
questions.explain: `mock.calls` is an array with one entry per call. Each entry is the list of arguments for that call.
wrong: Calls aren't flattened; each call keeps its own argument list.
That is the number of calls, which is `mock.calls.length`.
Only the arguments really passed are recorded; nothing is padded.

questions.q: What does this code log?
questions.explain: `mockReturnValueOnce` values are used first, in order. When they run out, the mock falls back to `mockReturnValue`.
wrong: The once values win over the default, even though the default was set first.
The default `6` is used after the once values run out.
The once values are used before the default.

questions.q: Which statement about this code is true?
options: `result` is 8, but the spy recorded no calls
`result` is 8, and the spy recorded a call with 4
`spyOn` throws, because `double` is an arrow function
questions.explain: By default `jest.spyOn` records calls and still runs the real method. So the result is real, and the call is tracked.
wrong: A spy only replaces the method if you add a mock implementation.
The call goes through the spy, so it is recorded.
Any function stored on an object can be spied on.

questions.q: `registerUser` should call `send('a@b.co', 'Welcome!')`. The test stays green even when that call is deleted. Which assertion should replace the last line?
questions.explain: A mock proves nothing until you assert how it was used. `toHaveBeenCalledWith` fails when the call is missing or has the wrong arguments.
wrong: This checks what `send` returned, and a plain mock returns `undefined`.
`expect.anything()` matches an empty array too, so it passes with no call.
A mock is always a function, called or not.

questions.q: Between tests, a developer wants every mock to keep its `mockReturnValue` setup but forget the calls it recorded. Which call fits?
questions.explain: `clearAllMocks` wipes each mock's call records (`mock.calls` and `mock.results`). It keeps the fake return values you set.
wrong: `resetAllMocks` also drops the fake return values.
`restoreAllMocks` is for putting spied original methods back.
`resetModules` clears the module cache, not mock call records.

questions.q: What does this code log?
questions.explain: `mockReturnValue` makes the spy return `'fake'` instead of running the real method. `mockRestore` then puts the original method back.
wrong: `mockRestore` brings back the real method for the second call.
The first call goes to the spy, which returns `'fake'`.
Restore brings back the original method, which returns `'real'`.

questions.q: What does this code log?
questions.explain: `resetAllMocks` wipes call records and the fake return value, so the mock returns `undefined`. The new call happens before `.length` is read, so it counts as 1.
wrong: Reset drops the `0.2` return value.
The call in `console.log` runs first, so one call is recorded.
Reset wiped the first call, and the return value is gone.

questions.q: `debounce(fn, ms)` waits `ms` after the last call, then calls `fn` once. Which assertion belongs on the last line?
questions.explain: Fake timers move time on command. After 500 ms in total, the debounced `save` runs once, because the two quick calls merge into one.
wrong: Debounce merges quick calls, so `save` runs once, not twice.
500 ms have passed, so `save` has run.
`save` gets the caller's arguments, not the delay.

questions.q: Why would a test call `jest.useFakeTimers()`?
options: To make every `setTimeout` throw an error
To slow tests down so they behave like a real, slow network
To run each test in its own browser tab
To run timer code without waiting for real time to pass
questions.explain: Fake timers replace `setTimeout` and friends. The test moves time forward itself, so nothing really waits.
wrong: Timers still work; they just wait for the test to move time.
Fake timers make tests faster, not slower.
Timers have nothing to do with browser tabs.

questions.q: `const log = jest.fn();` was then called once, with `'a'`. Which two assertions pass? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: `toHaveBeenCalledWith` checks the arguments of any call. `toHaveBeenNthCalledWith(1, 'a')` checks the first call; the 1 is the call number.
wrong: A plain `jest.fn()` returns `undefined`, not `'a'`.
The mock was called once, not twice.
`toHaveBeenLastCalledWith` takes only the arguments, so `1` is treated as one of them.

questions.q: In this CommonJS test file, `jest.mock('./api')` comes after the `require` lines. The project uses Jest's default `babel-jest` transform. What happens?
options: The mock still applies: `jest.mock` calls are hoisted to the top
The mock is ignored, because `./api` was already loaded with its real code
Jest throws an error, because `jest.mock` must come first
Only `getForecast` gets the mock; the `api` variable stays real
questions.explain: `babel-jest` moves (hoists) `jest.mock` calls to the top of the file, above the `require` lines. So both `weather.js` and the test get the mocked `api` module.
wrong: Hoisting runs the mock before any `require`, so the real module isn't used.
No error; the order in the file is fixed up for you.
Both files share one mocked copy of the module.

questions.q: `loadUser` calls `api.get('/me')`. Which two values for `fakeGet` let this test pass? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: `loadUser` calls `.then`, so `api.get` must return a promise. `mockResolvedValue(x)` is a shortcut for `mockImplementation(() => Promise.resolve(x))`.
wrong: A plain object has no `.then`, so `loadUser` throws.
A rejected promise makes `.resolves` fail.
It returns a plain object too, with no `.then`.

questions.q: Which kind of test double only hands back canned answers and keeps no record of how it was called?
questions.explain: A stub just gives ready-made answers. Spies and mocks also record or check how they were used.
wrong: A spy records the calls it receives.
A mock is set up with expected calls and is checked against them.
A fake timer controls time, not answers.

questions.q: `notify` works correctly, but the second test fails. Which two changes fix the tests without hiding real bugs? (Choose 2)
options: Create a new `mailer` with its own `jest.fn()` inside each test
questions.explain: The shared mock still holds the call from the first test. Clearing mocks before each test, or making a fresh mock per test, gives each test a clean record.
wrong: `afterAll` runs once at the very end, too late to help.
This is the same check, so it still sees the old call.
The test already has one assertion; the stale call is the problem.

questions.q: A test uses `jest.spyOn(api, 'send')` to check that `send` is called. But the real network call still happens during the test. Why?
options: `jest.spyOn` only works on class methods, not on plain objects
The spy must be created after the code calls `send`
`jest.spyOn` calls through to the real method by default
questions.explain: A Jest spy wraps the real method and still calls it by default. Add `.mockImplementation()` or `.mockResolvedValue()` to stop the real call.
wrong: `spyOn` works on any method stored on an object.
A spy created after the call misses that call entirely.
Spies don't depend on fake timers.
